**CO 1 ////// -- 1 Congenital Talipes Equinovarus CTEV / Clubfoot**

**Introduction**
**Definition** CTEV is a complex congenital deformity of the foot characterized by four distinct components Equinus plantarflexion at the ankle Varus inversion of the subtalar joint Adduction of the forefoot and Cavus exaggerated medial longitudinal arch It is commonly remembered by the mnemonic CAVE
**Clinical Features** The foot is turned downwards and inwards resembling a club Deep creases are visible on the medial border and posterior aspect of the heel The heel is small and empty calcaneus is pulled up The calf muscles especially on the affected side are visibly atrophied and underdeveloped It is a rigid deformity that cannot be passively corrected to a neutral position Can be unilateral or bilateral
**Investigations** Clinical Diagnosis Diagnosis is primarily clinical immediately at birth X rays AP and Lateral views of the foot in stress dorsiflexion Used to assess the severity and document the baseline bony alignment Kites angle talocalcaneal angle X rays are also used to monitor the progress of correction
**Complications** If untreated the child walks on the dorsolateral aspect of the foot Formation of painful large callosities and bursa over the weight bearing area Awkward limping gait Rocker bottom foot iatrogenic complication if the midfoot is forced into dorsiflexion before the heel equinus is corrected Severe psychological and cosmetic impact
**Medical / Conservative Management** Ponseti Method Gold Standard Serial manipulation and casting starting within the first week of life The deformities are corrected in a specific order Cavus Adductus Varus and finally Equinus Casts are changed weekly Splinting After full correction the foot is maintained in a Denis Browne splint or Foot Abduction Brace full time for 3 months then at night until 4 years of age to prevent relapse
**Surgical Management** Percutaneous Tendoachilles Tenotomy Often required as the final step of the Ponseti method to correct residual equinus Posteromedial Soft Tissue Release PMSTR Done for resistant or neglected cases in children 6 months to 2 years involving surgical release of tight medial and posterior ligaments/tendons Bony Surgeries For older neglected children e g wedge resection triple arthrodesis or Ilizarov ring fixator

---
**2 Congenital Dislocation of Hip CDH / DDH**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Now correctly termed Developmental Dysplasia of the Hip DDH this represents a spectrum of hip abnormalities ranging from a shallow dysplastic acetabulum to subluxation and completely dislocated femoral head
**Clinical Features** Neonates/Infants Asymmetrical thigh and gluteal skin folds Limited abduction of the affected hip Ortolani Test Positive A palpable clunk as the dislocated hip is reduced back into the socket during abduction Barlow Test Positive The hip can be dislocated out of the socket with posterior pressure and adduction Older Children Walking age Painless limp Shortening of the affected limb Galeazzi sign positive Waddling gait if bilateral or Trendelenburg lurch Trendelenburg test is positive pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the affected leg
**Investigations** Ultrasound Infants 6 months The investigation of choice because the femoral head is not yet ossified Used to assess acetabular depth and hip stability Grafs classification X rays Children 6 months An AP pelvis radiograph is used Pathological findings include a broken Shentons line an increased acetabular index and the femoral head lying outside the inner lower quadrant formed by Hilgenreiners and Perkins lines
**Complications** Avascular Necrosis AVN of the femoral head often iatrogenic from forced abduction Premature osteoarthritis of the hip in young adulthood Permanent limb length discrepancy and limping Severe limp and compensatory scoliosis
**Medical / Conservative Management** Birth to 6 months Pavlik harness A dynamic splint that maintains the hips in flexion and abduction keeping the femoral head centered in the acetabulum to allow it to deepen naturally 6 to 18 months Closed reduction under general anesthesia followed by a Hip Spica cast for 3 6 months
**Surgical Management** Open Reduction Indicated if closed reduction fails or for children presenting late 18 months Soft tissues preventing reduction are cleared out Pelvic Osteotomies e g Salter Pemberton To re orient the shallow acetabulum to better cover the femoral head Femoral Derotation/Shortening Osteotomies To relieve pressure on the joint and prevent AVN

---
**3 Torticollis Congenital Muscular Torticollis**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Congenital Muscular Torticollis Wry neck is a deformity characterized by a lateral tilt of the head to one side and rotation of the chin to the opposite side caused by unilateral fibrosis and shortening of the sternocleidomastoid SCM muscle
**Clinical Features** Head is tilted toward the side of the contracted muscle and the chin points away from it In the first few weeks of life a firm painless swelling sternomastoid tumor or olive may be palpable in the belly of the SCM muscle This mass resolves over months but leaves a fibrous band Restricted neck range of motion Plagiocephaly Flattening of the face and skull on one side due to consistent sleeping posture if left untreated
**Investigations** Clinical Diagnosis is primarily clinical Ultrasound Can confirm the fibrotic mass within the SCM muscle X rays of Cervical Spine Mandatory to rule out bony congenital anomalies of the spine like Klippel Feil syndrome or hemivertebrae that can also cause a wry neck
**Complications** Permanent facial asymmetry hemi hypoplasia of the face Compensatory cervical scoliosis Vision problems strabismus due to abnormal head posture Psychological issues due to cosmetic deformity
**Medical / Conservative Management** Physiotherapy Gentle passive stretching exercises of the neck performed by parents multiple times a day Positioning Placing toys or positioning the crib so the child is forced to look away from the preferred side actively stretching the muscle Over 90 of cases resolve completely with early conservative management within the first year of life
**Surgical Management** Indications Failure of conservative treatment after 1 year of age or presentation in an older child Procedure Surgical release tenotomy of the sternocleidomastoid muscle unipolar release at the clavicle/sternum or bipolar release including the mastoid attachment Followed by a corrective brace/collar and aggressive physiotherapy

---
**4 Scoliosis Congenital and Idiopathic**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Scoliosis is defined as a complex 3 dimensional deformity of the spine characterized by a lateral curvature in the coronal plane exceeding 10 degrees accompanied by vertebral rotation Congenital scoliosis is caused by bony anomalies like hemivertebrae while idiopathic is of unknown cause
**Clinical Features** Usually painless pain is a red flag for tumors or tethered cord Asymmetrical shoulder height Prominent or protruding scapula on one side Asymmetry of the waistline creases Adams Forward Bending Test Pathognomonic sign is a rib hump on the convex side of the curve caused by vertebral rotation pushing the ribs backward
**Investigations** X rays Standing AP and Lateral of whole spine Confirms diagnosis The severity of the curve is measured using Cobbs angle MRI of the Spine Essential especially in congenital or early onset scoliosis to rule out intra spinal anomalies syringomyelia tethered cord Arnold Chiari malformation
**Complications** Cardiopulmonary compromise Cor Pulmonale Severe thoracic curves 90 degrees severely restrict lung capacity leading to right heart failure and reduced life expectancy Severe cosmetic deformity and psychological distress Back pain and degenerative arthritis in adulthood Neurological deficits rare but possible in rapidly progressive congenital curves
**Medical / Conservative Management** Observation Curves 20 degrees are observed with serial X rays every 6 months Bracing e g Boston brace Milwaukee brace Indicated for flexible curves between 20 to 40 degrees in growing children Braces do not correct the curve but aim to halt its progression until skeletal maturity
**Surgical Management** Indications Curves 45 50 degrees documented rapid progression or significant cosmetic/respiratory impairment Procedure Posterior Spinal Fusion with instrumentation pedicle screws hooks and rods to correct the curve and fuse the spine in the corrected position In congenital scoliosis hemivertebra excision and short segment fusion may be done early

---
**5 Flat Foot Pes Planus**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Flat foot is the loss or collapse of the medial longitudinal arch of the foot resulting in the medial border of the foot coming into contact with the ground It can be flexible arch appears when non weight bearing or on tiptoes or rigid arch is absent constantly
**Clinical Features** Medial border of the foot touches the floor when standing Heel is usually in a valgus position outward deviation Flexible Flat Foot Arch reconstitutes when the patient stands on their tiptoes or when the great toe is passively dorsiflexed Jacks test Usually painless Rigid Flat Foot Arch does not reconstitute Often painful with severe restriction of subtalar joint movement Commonly caused by tarsal coalition fusion of foot bones
**Investigations** Weight bearing X rays AP and Lateral Lateral view shows the collapse of the arch Mearys angle angle between the talus and first metatarsal is increased CT Scan The best modality to diagnose a tarsal coalition in rigid flat feet
**Complications** Foot fatigue and cramping in the calves after walking or running Abnormal wear of shoes wearing out the inner border Predisposition to developing Hallux Valgus bunions or Plantar Fasciitis Chronic foot pain and stiffness in rigid types
**Medical / Conservative Management** Flexible Asymptomatic Reassurance only It is a normal variant in toddlers No treatment is needed Flexible Symptomatic Custom arch supports orthotics medial heel wedges and Achilles tendon stretching exercises to relieve fatigue Rigid Immobilization in a cast or use of rigid orthotics to reduce inflammation and pain
**Surgical Management** Indications Severe painful flat feet failing conservative treatment Flexible Calcaneal lengthening osteotomies or tendon transfers repair of tibialis posterior Rigid Tarsal Coalition Resection of the coalition block If severe arthritis is present a triple arthrodesis fusion of the subtalar talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints is performed

---
**6 Vertical Talus Congenital Convex Pes Valgus**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Congenital Vertical Talus is a rare severe and rigid flatfoot deformity present at birth The talus bone is fixed in an extreme vertical plantarflexed position and the navicular bone is dorsally dislocated over the neck of the talus locking it in place
**Clinical Features** Rocker bottom deformity The sole of the foot is convex rather than concave The forefoot is dorsiflexed and abducted The hindfoot heel is fixed in equinus pulled up The head of the talus forms a prominent hard peg like bump on the plantar medial aspect of the sole The deformity is rigidly fixed
**Investigations** Lateral X ray in maximum plantarflexion This is diagnostic In a vertical talus the navicular or the first metatarsal axis if the navicular is not ossified does not align with the axis of the talus even when the foot is forced into plantarflexion
**Complications** If untreated the child walks directly on the head of the talus Formation of massive painful callosities and ulcerations on the sole Inability to wear normal shoes Severe permanent gait disability and foot pain
**Medical / Conservative Management** Unlike flexible flat feet or clubfeet conservative management alone is rarely curative Serial Casting The reverse Ponseti casting method is used initially to stretch the dorsal and lateral soft tissues to make eventual surgery less extensive
**Surgical Management** Surgery is almost always required ideally before the child reaches walking age 6 12 months Open Reduction Extensive soft tissue releases reduction of the talonavicular joint and pinning with Kirschner wires K wires Minimally Invasive Dobbs method serial casting followed by percutaneous pinning and Achilles tenotomy Salvage Talectomy removal of talus or triple arthrodesis in severely neglected older children

---
**7 Hand Anomalies Syndactyly Polydactyly Ectrodactyly**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Syndactyly Failure of separation of adjacent digits webbed fingers Polydactyly Presence of extra supernumerary digits Ectrodactyly Cleft hand or lobster claw deformity characterized by a central V shaped cleft and missing central digits
**Clinical Features** Syndactyly Digits are fused It can be simple only skin/soft tissue fused or complex bones and joints are fused Can be complete up to the fingertips or incomplete Polydactyly Extra digits can be Preaxial on the thumb/radial side or Postaxial on the little finger/ulnar side Ranges from a floppy skin tag to a fully functional digit with its own joints and tendons Ectrodactyly Missing middle finger/metacarpals with the remaining fingers separated by a deep central cleft severely altering hand appearance
**Investigations** Plain X rays of the Hand Mandatory to define the bony anatomy confirm if joints are shared complex syndactyly and see if the extra digit in polydactyly has bony support or is just a soft tissue appendage
**Complications** Severe psychological and social stigma due to cosmetic appearance Reduced hand span and grip strength In syndactyly if digits of unequal length e g thumb and index are tethered together it restricts the growth of the longer digit leading to joint deviation and contractures
**Medical / Conservative Management** Occupational therapy for adaptive training and maximizing hand function Splinting to prevent contractures in awaiting surgical candidates
**Surgical Management** Syndactyly Surgical separation web space reconstruction using zig zag incisions and full thickness skin grafts Done early around 6 12 months if unequal digits are fused to prevent growth tethering Polydactyly Surgical excision of the extra digit If the extra digit shares a joint with the normal digit careful reconstruction of collateral ligaments and tendons is required to ensure the remaining digit is stable Ectrodactyly Surgical closure of the cleft transposition of digits and soft tissue releases to improve pinch function and cosmetic appearance

---
**8 Arthrogryposis Multiplex Congenita AMC / Amyoplasia Congenita**

**Introduction**
**Definition** AMC is a non progressive congenital syndrome characterized by multiple severe rigid joint contractures present at birth in two or more areas of the body It is associated with the replacement of normal skeletal muscle with fibrous and fatty tissue
**Clinical Features** Joints Limbs appear wooden or rigid The joints lack normal creases and instead have dimples over them Classic Posture Shoulders internally rotated elbows fixed in extension wrists flexed and ulnarly deviated hips dislocated knees extended and severe rigid clubfeet Sensation and intelligence are completely normal Skin is tense and lacks normal subcutaneous tissue
**Investigations** Clinical Strongly clinical diagnosis based on multiple joint involvement X rays To check for joint dislocations especially hips and assess bony alignment Muscle Biopsy/EMG May be done to differentiate from progressive muscular dystrophies or spinal muscular atrophy showing fibrofatty replacement of muscle
**Complications** Extreme difficulty with activities of daily living inability to feed oneself if elbows are fixed in extension Inability to walk due to hip dislocations and rigid feet High risk of iatrogenic fractures if joints are manipulated too forcefully during physical therapy Development of secondary scoliosis
**Medical / Conservative Management** Must begin immediately after birth Aggressive daily passive stretching and physical therapy to maximize whatever limited joint motion exists Serial casting and custom thermoplastic splints to hold the joints in corrected positions
**Surgical Management** Goal Not to restore normal motion which is impossible but to place the limbs in functional positions Upper Limb Soft tissue releases or osteotomies to flex the elbows so the child can reach their mouth to eat and fuse/stabilize the wrists Lower Limb Relocation of hips releasing knee contractures and extensive bony surgeries talectomies osteotomies to make the feet plantigrade so the child can stand

---
**9 Limb Deficiencies Amelia and Phocomelia**

**Introduction**
**Definition** These are severe congenital failures of limb formation Amelia The complete absence of one or more limbs transverse deficiency Phocomelia A longitudinal deficiency where the proximal segments of the limb arm/bone are absent or severely hypoplastic but the distal hand or foot is attached directly to the trunk resembling the flippers of a seal Historically linked to the maternal use of Thalidomide
**Clinical Features** Profound visibly obvious absence of limb segments at birth In phocomelia the attached digits may be deformed or functionally impaired but patients often develop extraordinary dexterity with them General health and intellect are usually unaffected though associated organ anomalies can occur
**Investigations** X rays To accurately map the residual skeletal anatomy and identify which bones are completely absent versus hypoplastic Systemic Ultrasound/ECHO To rule out associated visceral anomalies cardiac renal gastrointestinal
**Complications** Severe impairment of independent mobility and self care Extreme psychological and emotional challenges for the patient and parents Difficulty fitting standard prostheses due to the lack of a normal residual stump Skeletal imbalances leading to severe scoliosis
**Medical / Conservative Management** Intense Occupational/Physical Therapy Training to use remaining limbs or other body parts e g using feet for writing or feeding to achieve independence Prosthetics The mainstay of treatment Myoelectric arms or body powered prosthetics Fitting begins early around 6 months so the child integrates the prosthesis into their body image
**Surgical Management** Reconstructive surgery is limited due to the sheer lack of tissue Amputations Occasionally non functional flail digits in phocomelia are amputated to allow a modern prosthesis to fit better over the stump Rotationplasty In specific lower limb deficiencies like PFFD the leg is rotated 180 degrees so the ankle joint functions as a knee joint within a prosthesis

---
**10 Klippel Feil Syndrome**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Klippel Feil Syndrome is a congenital malformation characterized by the failure of segmentation fusion of two or more cervical vertebrae
**Clinical Features** Classic Triad Present in 50 of cases Short neck Low posterior hairline Markedly restricted range of motion of the neck Webbed Neck Pterygium colli may be visually apparent Sprengels Deformity Congenital undescended high riding scapula is present in about 30 of patients Neurological symptoms are usually absent in childhood but can develop later in life
**Investigations** X rays Cervical Spine Shows the block vertebrae fused vertebral bodies absent disc spaces and often associated hemivertebrae MRI Spine Mandatory to check for associated spinal cord anomalies like syringomyelia tethered cord or diastematomyelia Ultrasound/ECHO To check for common associated anomalies renal agenesis congenital heart defects
**Complications** Cervical Instability The unfused segments adjacent to the fused blocks become hypermobile to compensate This hypermobility leads to early severe degenerative changes and instability Neurological Injury Minor trauma can cause fatal or paralyzing spinal cord compression at the hypermobile segments Deafness common association
**Medical / Conservative Management** Activity Restriction Absolute avoidance of contact sports gymnastics or activities with a risk of head/neck trauma Observation and symptomatic treatment NSAIDs gentle physical therapy for mechanical neck pain
**Surgical Management** Prophylactic Spinal Fusion Indicated if there is documented dangerous instability at the cervical segments adjacent to the fusion block or if there is progressive neurological deficit Woodward or Green Procedure Surgical relocation of the scapula downwards if an associated Sprengels deformity is causing severe cosmetic or functional impairment

---
**11 Osteogenesis Imperfecta Fragile Ossium**

**Introduction**
**Definition** Osteogenesis Imperfecta Brittle Bone Disease is a genetic disorder of connective tissue caused by mutations in the genes COL1A1/COL1A2 responsible for producing Type I collagen This results in severe osteopenia and extreme bone fragility
**Clinical Features** Multiple Fractures Occur from minimal or no trauma Even routine diaper changing can cause femur fractures in severe types Blue Sclerae The sclera of the eyes appear blue/gray because the thin scleral collagen allows the underlying choroid pigment to show through Dentinogenesis Imperfecta Teeth are discolored yellow/brown translucent and prone to rapid wear and breakage Deformities Severe bowing of long bones due to microfractures and soft bone Joint hypermobility and hearing loss otosclerosis in adulthood
**Investigations** X rays Reveal severe generalized osteopenia extremely thin cortices multiple healing fractures at various stages severe bowing of long bones and sometimes popcorn calcifications in the metaphyses DEXA Scan To quantify the severe reduction in bone mineral density Genetic Testing Confirms the specific collagen mutation
**Complications** Severe crippling skeletal deformities leading to wheelchair dependence Extreme short stature dwarfism Non unions or severe malunions of fractures Basilar Invagination The soft skull base settles onto the cervical spine causing life threatening compression of the brainstem and spinal cord
**Medical / Conservative Management** Bisphosphonates e g IV Pamidronate or Zoledronic acid are the medical mainstay They inhibit osteoclast activity significantly increasing bone density reducing pain and decreasing the fracture rate Careful handling of the infant lifting by the trunk never by the limbs Lightweight bracing to support bowed limbs
**Surgical Management** Intramedullary Rodding Standard surgery for repeated fractures and bowing The bone is cut into segments osteotomies straightened like beads on a string and fixed with an intramedullary rod Telescopic Rods Fassier Duval rods Specialized rods that expand as the child grows preventing the bone from growing past the rod and fracturing at the tip Avoid Plates Traditional plates and screws are avoided as the screws easily pull out of the fragile bone

---
**12 Cervical Rib**

**Introduction**
**Definition** A cervical rib is a congenital supernumerary extra rib that arises from the transverse process of the seventh cervical vertebra C7 It can be a fully formed bony rib or a fibrous band attaching to the first rib potentially causing compression in the thoracic outlet
**Clinical Features** The vast majority are entirely asymptomatic and found incidentally Thoracic Outlet Syndrome TOS If symptomatic it causes compression of the brachial plexus C8 T1 nerve roots and the subclavian artery/vein Neurological Pain tingling and numbness along the ulnar border of the forearm and hand Weakness clumsiness and wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the hand thenar and hypothenar eminences Vascular The hand becomes cold pale and pulseless especially when the arm is raised Adsons Test Positive radial pulse disappears upon taking a deep breath and turning the head toward the affected side
**Investigations** X rays AP Neck/Chest Identifies the presence of a bony cervical rib or an elongated C7 transverse process Nerve Conduction Studies EMG/NCV Confirms neurological compression at the thoracic outlet differentiating it from ulnar neuropathy at the elbow Doppler Ultrasound / Angiography Used if vascular compression or a subclavian artery aneurysm is suspected
**Complications** Severe intractable neurogenic pain Permanent wasting and loss of function of hand muscles Vascular Post stenotic dilatation of the subclavian artery leading to aneurysm formation thrombosis and distal embolization causing gangrene of the fingertips
**Medical / Conservative Management** First line treatment for purely neurological mild symptoms Physiotherapy Specific exercises aimed at strengthening the shoulder girdle muscles trapezius levator scapulae to elevate the shoulder and open up the thoracic outlet space Postural correction avoiding slouching NSAIDs for pain relief
**Surgical Management** Indications Failure of 3 6 months of conservative therapy progressive muscle wasting or any signs of vascular compression ischemia aneurysm Procedure Surgical excision of the cervical rib or the fibrous band along with the division of the scalenus anterior muscle scaleneotomy This thoroughly decompresses the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery ///////////

---
**1 ACQUIRED TORTICOLLIS**

**DEFINITION** Acquired torticollis is a condition in which the head assumes an abnormal position due to shortening spasm pain or dysfunction of the cervical muscles producing lateral flexion of the head to one side with rotation of the chin toward the opposite side
**CAUSES**
- Muscular causes
- Sternocleidomastoid spasm
- Cervical muscle strain
- Myofascial pain
- Trauma
- Whiplash injury
- Cervical fracture/dislocation
- Infection
- Retropharyngeal abscess
- Cervical tuberculosis
- Neurological causes
- Dystonia
- Cerebral lesions
- Ocular causes
- Abnormal ocular alignment
- Cervical spine disorders
- Cervical spondylosis
- Disc prolapse
- Inflammatory conditions
- Rheumatoid arthritis
- Postural causes

**CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Head tilted to one side
- Chin rotated toward opposite side
- Neck pain
- Cervical muscle spasm
- Restricted cervical ROM
- Tenderness
- Shoulder asymmetry
- Difficulty turning the head
- Headache may occur
- In chronic cases facial asymmetry may develop

**COMPLICATIONS**
- Persistent neck pain
- Cervical stiffness
- Muscle shortening
- Postural deformity
- Headache
- Secondary scoliosis
- Functional limitation

**INVESTIGATIONS**
- Cervical spine X ray
- CT/MRI when structural pathology is suspected
- Neurological examination
- Blood investigations when infection/inflammation is suspected

**CONSERVATIVE/MEDICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Treatment of underlying cause
- Analgesics/NSAIDs
- Heat therapy
- Gentle cervical ROM
- Stretching of shortened muscles
- Strengthening of weak muscles
- Postural correction
- Cervical traction in selected cases
- Soft cervical collar for short term use when appropriate
- Botulinum toxin for selected dystonic torticollis

**SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
Indicated when severe fixed deformity or structural pathology persists
- Sternocleidomastoid release/lengthening
- Muscle/tendon release
- Cervical decompression or stabilization when indicated by underlying pathology

**FLOW CHART**
Underlying cause muscle spasm/shortening abnormal head position restricted ROM chronic deformity functional limitation

---
**2 ACQUIRED SCOLIOSIS**

**DEFINITION** Scoliosis is a three dimensional deformity of the spine characterized by lateral curvature associated with vertebral rotation generally measured by the Cobb angle on radiographs Acquired scoliosis develops after birth due to a known or secondary cause
**CAUSES**
- Poor posture
- Leg length discrepancy
- Muscle imbalance
- Cerebral palsy
- Muscular dystrophy
- Poliomyelitis
- Spinal tuberculosis
- Vertebral fracture
- Tumors
- Degenerative spinal disease
- Painful conditions
- Trauma

**CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Unequal shoulder height
- Unequal scapular prominence
- Unequal waist contours
- Pelvic asymmetry
- Lateral spinal curvature
- Rib prominence
- Trunk shift
- Back pain particularly in degenerative scoliosis
- Reduced spinal mobility
- Leg length discrepancy may be present

**CLINICAL TEST**
Adams forward bending test Patient bends forward Rib hump or lumbar prominence suggests vertebral rotation

**COMPLICATIONS**
- Chronic back pain
- Progressive deformity
- Reduced pulmonary function in severe curves
- Reduced exercise tolerance
- Neurological compromise in selected structural causes
- Psychological/social problems
- Functional disability

**RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES**
Standing AP/PA and lateral spine radiographs demonstrate Lateral curvature Vertebral rotation Cobb angle Vertebral wedging Degenerative changes where applicable

**CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT**
Treat underlying cause
- Physiotherapy
- Postural correction
- Core strengthening
- Spinal mobility exercises
- Stretching
- Breathing exercises
- Bracing in selected growing patients
- Leg length correction if discrepancy contributes
- Analgesics for pain

**SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
Indications depend on severity progression symptoms and cause
- Spinal instrumentation and fusion
- Corrective osteotomy in selected rigid deformities
- Decompression if neurological compression exists
- Treatment of underlying tumor/infection when responsible

**FLOW CHART**
Underlying condition muscle imbalance/vertebral pathology lateral curvature rotation progressive deformity pain/functional impairment

---
**3 KYPHOSIS**

**DEFINITION** Kyphosis is an excessive posterior convex curvature of the thoracic or thoracolumbar spine producing an exaggerated rounded back appearance
**CAUSES**
- Poor posture
- Osteoporosis
- Vertebral compression fractures
- Scheuermann disease
- Tuberculosis of spine
- Degenerative disease
- Trauma
- Tumor
- Neuromuscular disorders
- Ankylosing spondylitis

**CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Rounded back
- Forward head posture
- Increased thoracic curvature
- Shoulder protraction
- Back pain
- Hamstring tightness may occur
- Reduced spinal mobility
- Reduced chest expansion in severe cases
- Fatigue
- Neurological symptoms in severe structural disease

**COMPLICATIONS**
- Chronic pain
- Progressive deformity
- Restrictive respiratory impairment
- Reduced balance
- Increased fall risk
- Neurological compression
- Spinal cord injury in severe cases

**RADIOLOGICAL FEATURES**
- Increased thoracic kyphotic angle
- Vertebral wedging
- Compression fractures
- Degenerative changes
- Vertebral destruction in infective disease

**CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT**
- Postural education
- Thoracic extension exercises
- Back extensor strengthening
- Abdominal strengthening
- Stretching of pectoral muscles
- Breathing exercises
- Analgesics
- Osteoporosis management
- Bracing in selected patients

**SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
- Vertebral augmentation in selected painful compression fractures
- Corrective osteotomy
- Spinal fusion
- Decompression and stabilization when neurological compression/instability is present

---
**4 LORDOSIS**

**DEFINITION** Lordosis is an excessive anterior convex curvature of the spine most commonly affecting the lumbar region
**CAUSES**
- Obesity
- Pregnancy
- Weak abdominal muscles
- Tight hip flexors
- Spondylolisthesis
- Hip flexion deformity
- Osteoporosis
- Spinal deformity
- Poor posture
- Neuromuscular disorders

**CLINICAL FEATURES**
- Increased lumbar curvature
- Anterior pelvic tilt
- Protruding abdomen
- Prominent buttocks
- Low back pain
- Tight hip flexors
- Weak abdominal/gluteal muscles
- Hamstring dysfunction may occur

**COMPLICATIONS**
- Chronic low back pain
- Facet joint stress
- Muscle fatigue
- Reduced mobility
- Secondary disc/facet degeneration
- Neurological symptoms if associated with spinal pathology

**CONSERVATIVE MANAGEMENT**
- Postural correction
- Abdominal strengthening
- Gluteal strengthening
- Hip flexor stretching
- Hamstring stretching when appropriate
- Core stabilization
- Weight management
- Ergonomic modification
- Analgesia

**SURGICAL MANAGEMENT**
Surgery is directed at the underlying cause
- Decompression
- Spinal stabilization/fusion
- Corrective osteotomy
- Treatment of spondylolisthesis when indicated

---
**5 GENU VARUM**

**DEFINITION** Genu varum or bow legs is a deformity in which the knees remain separated when the ankles are brought together producing an outward angulation of the legs
**CAUSES**
- Physiological deformity
- Rickets
- Blount disease
- Malunited fractures
- Growth plate injury
